## Choose **one** prompt to answer

> **Prompt C:** `r params$p3`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->

When researchers try to interpret words, images, or messages in things like latent coding or sentiment analysis, they’re basically making judgment calls and those choices can cause big problems if they get something wrong. If they misread someone’s tone or intention, the whole meaning of the data can be misunderstood. For example, sarcasm or jokes might get labeled as “negative” or “angry,” even though the person was actually trying to be funny. Cultural differences in language can be misunderstood too, which makes the results even less accurate. The chapter talks about how these kinds of mistakes can mess with the validity and fairness of a study. This is true in topics like identity, politics, or public opinion, where people express themselves in more complicated and personal ways. If researchers or computer programs mislabel certain groups more than others, it can make it look like those groups say things they really didn’t or it might make their real views disappear from the data. This is why training really matters. Human coders need practice, clear definitions, and tests to make sure they’re all coding things the same way. The chapter also explains that checking inter-coder reliability helps make sure nobody is interpreting the rules too loosely. For computer models, the training data has to be diverse and coded correctly, or the algorithm will just repeat whatever bias it learned, which can make the results unfair. Overall, good training helps protect research from becoming inaccurate or biased. It makes sure that the way messages are interpreted actually reflects what people meant, not just what the researchers think they meant. <!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
